DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: UpSafe$^\circ$C: Upcycling for Controllable Safety in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety through a unified framework that balances safety, utility, and controllability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes UPSAFE°C, a safety-aware upcycling framework that identifies safety-critical layers, converts them into a sparse MoE structure with a soft guardrail router, and introduces a safety temperature for inference-time control, achieving robust safety improvements while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: UPSAFE°C offers a novel direction for LLM safety by shifting from static alignment toward dynamic, modular, and inference-aware control, achieving a favorable balance between safety and utility.
papers.key_findings:
UPSAFE°C significantly enhances safety performance on benchmarks like JBB, StrongReject, WildChat, and WildJailbreak, often reaching 100% safety rates.
The method maintains or improves general capabilities on tasks like HumanEval, MMLU, and Math-500 compared to baselines.
The safety temperature mechanism provides fine-grained inference-time control, allowing dynamic adjustment of the safety-utility trade-off and achieving Pareto-optimal frontiers.
The router acts as an effective soft guardrail, selectively activating safety experts for harmful inputs and the general expert for benign inputs.
Ablation studies show the importance of the safety-critical layer scan, the two-stage training strategy, and a moderate number of safety experts for optimal performance.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of tasks, but remain vulnerable to safety risks such as harmful content generation and jailbreak attacks. Existing safety techniques -- including external guardrails, inference-time guidance, and post-training alignment -- each face limitations in balancing safety, utility, and controllability. In this work, we propose UpSafe$^\circ$C, a unified framework for enhancing LLM safety through safety-aware upcycling. Our approach first identifies safety-critical layers and upcycles them into a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) structure, where the router acts as a soft guardrail that selectively activates original MLPs and added safety experts. We further introduce a two-stage SFT strategy to strengthen safety discrimination while preserving general capabilities. To enable flexible control at inference time, we introduce a safety temperature mechanism, allowing dynamic adjustment of the trade-off between safety and utility. Experiments across multiple benchmarks, base model, and model scales demonstrate that UpSafe$^\circ$C achieves robust safety improvements against harmful and jailbreak inputs, while maintaining competitive performance on general tasks. Moreover, analysis shows that safety temperature provides fine-grained inference-time control that achieves the Pareto-optimal frontier between utility and safety. Our results highlight a new direction for LLM safety: moving from static alignment toward dynamic, modular, and inference-aware control.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
papers.research_question: How universal are refusal directions across languages? Specifically, does a refusal direction extracted from one language transfer to others?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages; a refusal vector extracted from one language can effectively modulate refusal behavior in other languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages, providing insights for multilingual safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
English-derived refusal vectors can jailbreak models across multiple languages.
Refusal vectors derived from any safety-aligned language (e.g., German, Chinese, Thai) transfer to other languages.
The universality is due to parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space.
Models fail to separate harmful and harmless prompts in non-English languages, leading to vulnerabilities.
Adding refusal vectors can reduce compliance rates, demonstrating controllability.
papers.abstract: Refusal mechanisms in large language models (LLMs) are essential for ensuring safety. Recent research has revealed that refusal behavior can be mediated by a single direction in activation space, enabling targeted interventions to bypass refusals. While this is primarily demonstrated in an English-centric context, appropriate refusal behavior is important for any language, but poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the refusal behavior in LLMs across 14 languages using PolyRefuse, a multilingual safety dataset created by translating malicious and benign English prompts into these languages. We uncover the surprising cross-lingual universality of the refusal direction: a vector extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness, without any additional fine-tuning. Even more remarkably, refusal directions derived from any safety-aligned language transfer seamlessly to others. We attribute this transferability to the parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space and identify the underlying mechanism behind cross-lingual jailbreaks. These findings provide actionable insights for building more robust multilingual safety defenses and pave the way for a deeper mechanistic understanding of cross-lingual vulnerabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning
papers.research_question: How can refusal behavior in safety-aligned language models be ablated without causing collateral damage to core capabilities like math and coding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA), a method that cleans refusal vectors by orthogonalizing against capability and style directions, enabling precise ablation of refusal behavior with minimal distribution drift and preserved capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SRA treats refusal ablation as a semantic disentanglement problem, achieving behavioral editing with dramatically reduced drift and preserved capabilities compared to standard methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0–2% on harmful suite) with negligible perplexity impact on wikitext_2_raw and minimal distribution drift.
Standard ablation induces severe distribution drift, while SRA maintains original distribution while achieving low refusal rates.
SRA preserves or improves math and code perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP datasets.
The dirty refusal vector is polysemantic, entangling refusal signals with unrelated linguistic structure and capability circuits.
Cleaning the vector via spectral residualization reduces 'Ghost Noise' damage caused by standard ablation.
papers.limitation:
The atom registry is curated and may miss confounds; unseen entanglers could still leak into the refusal direction.
Evaluation limitations include refusal detection being definition-dependent, finite harmful prompt suites, and proxy drift metrics not substituting for comprehensive behavioral evaluation.
future_direction: Automating atom discovery or expanding registries to handle unseen confounds.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models systematically refuse harmful requests. While activation steering can modulate refusal, ablating the raw "refusal vector" calculated from contrastive harmful and harmless prompts often causes collateral damage and distribution drift. We argue this degradation occurs because the raw vector is polysemantic, entangling the refusal signal with core capability circuits and linguistic style. We introduce Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA) to distill these steering directions. SRA constructs a registry of independent Concept Atoms representing protected capabilities and stylistic confounds, then uses ridge-regularized spectral residualization to orthogonalize the refusal vector against these directions. This yields a clean refusal direction that targets refusal-relevant structure while minimizing disruption to the model's semantic geometry. Across five models (Qwen3-VL and Ministral series), SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0-2%) with negligible perplexity impact on Wikitext-2 (mean delta PPL approx. 0.02) and minimal distribution drift. Notably, standard ablation on Qwen3-VL-4B induces severe drift (first-token KL = 2.088), whereas SRA maintains the original distribution (KL = 0.044) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate. Using teacher-forced perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP as a high-resolution capability proxy, we show SRA preserves math and code distributions. These results suggest that common "model damage" is often "Ghost Noise," defined as the spectral bleeding of the dirty refusal direction into capability subspaces.

papers.title: Learnable Privacy Neurons Localization in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) memorize Personally Identifiable Information (PII), and can we localize the specific neurons responsible for this memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to localize PII-sensitive neurons in LLMs using learnable binary weight masks and adversarial training, demonstrating that PII memorization is concentrated in a small, specific subset of neurons, primarily in MLP layers, and that deactivating these neurons can mitigate privacy leakage.
papers.conclusion: The proposed neuron localization method advances the understanding of LLMs' inner mechanisms for PII memorization and offers a practical approach to enhancing privacy safeguards.
papers.key_findings:
PII memorization is localized to a small subset of neurons spread across all layers of the model.
Privacy neurons are predominantly located within the MLP layers of the transformer.
Privacy neurons exhibit specificity for different categories of PII knowledge.
Deactivating the localized privacy neurons significantly reduces PII leakage metrics (MA and EL) while largely preserving the model's general language modeling performance.
Approximately 3.5% of neurons are required to eliminate PII memorization, but masking beyond ~2% of neurons starts to affect general knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates the localization of PII memorization; other kinds of (privacy) information may possess a different pattern.
Experiments have not been conducted on very large models.
Experiments on privacy leakage mitigation are still preliminary.
future_direction: Extend the proposed method to the localization of other knowledge in LLMs.
Focus on the scalability of the neuron localization algorithm to larger models and broader applications.
Involve unlearning or knowledge editing techniques to enhance privacy leakage mitigation performance and use more evaluating datasets for comprehensive evaluation.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Just Enough Shifts: Mitigating Over-Refusal in Aligned Language Models with Targeted Representation Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate over-refusals (unnecessary rejections of benign prompts) in safety-aligned language models while preserving their ability to refuse genuinely harmful queries and maintaining overall utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ACTOR, a data- and compute-efficient training framework that reduces over-refusals by fine-tuning a single transformer layer to shift internal activations based on a computed refusal vector and query-specific projection targets.
papers.conclusion: ACTOR effectively balances over-refusal reduction and safety preservation by directly optimizing internal activation patterns, offering a powerful and efficient alternative to traditional response-based fine-tuning methods.
papers.key_findings:
ACTOR significantly improves compliance rates on over-refusal benchmarks while maintaining high safety scores on harmful queries.
ACTOR is more data- and compute-efficient than full supervised fine-tuning, requiring only query activations and fine-tuning a single layer.
ACTOR is distributionally robust, maintaining performance across different data distributions used to compute the refusal vector, unlike inference-time steering methods.
ACTOR preserves general model capabilities (knowledge, instruction-following, perplexity) with minimal degradation.
The method's 'just enough' shift, based on the projection of a query's activation onto the refusal vector, is more effective than applying uniform shifts.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is based on public benchmarks with inherent label disagreements about what constitutes 'safe' content, reflecting a compromise among embedded normative preferences rather than a universal safety notion.
ACTOR requires white-box access to model activations and an existing safety-alignment mechanism, limiting its use for third-party users of black-box APIs.
future_direction: Jointly curating data and fine-tuning the model, rather than optimizing against fixed benchmarks.
Extending evaluation to multi-turn dialogue scenarios, which currently lack dedicated benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is crucial for large language models (LLMs) to resist malicious instructions but often results in over-refusals, where benign prompts are unnecessarily rejected, impairing user experience and model utility. We introduce ACTOR (Activation-Based Training for Over-Refusal Reduction), a robust and compute- and data-efficient training framework that minimizes over-refusals by leveraging internal activation patterns from diverse queries. ACTOR precisely identifies and adjusts the activation components that trigger refusals, providing stronger control over the refusal mechanism. By fine-tuning only a single model layer, ACTOR effectively reduces over-refusals across multiple benchmarks while maintaining the model's ability to handle harmful queries and preserve overall utility.

papers.title: Understanding Language Model Circuits through Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How is knowledge structured within the critical subnetworks (circuits) of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines knowledge editing and circuit analysis to reveal that knowledge-intensive circuits exhibit 'confirmation bias' (resistance to editing), knowledge is distributed in circuits of intermediate size, circuits from different tasks overlap, and LayerNorm plays a larger role in circuits than previously assumed.
papers.conclusion: Combining knowledge editing and circuit analysis reveals novel properties of circuits, such as resistance to editing, distribution patterns, and the role of LayerNorm, supporting future explorations into model behaviors, bias removal, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-intensive circuits show stronger resistance to editing compared to their complementary parts, analogous to 'confirmation bias'.
Knowledge is neither extremely concentrated nor widely dispersed; ideal knowledge-bearing circuits likely contain between 5% and 50% of parameters.
Circuits extracted from different tasks (e.g., linguistic and knowledge-based) show non-negligible overlap.
LayerNorm components constitute a larger share of the extracted circuits than attention and MLP layers.
Complementary circuits are more susceptible to editing, suggesting potential for bias removal without compromising primary circuit performance.
papers.limitation:
Only the GPT-2 model was used.
Only fine-tuning model edit was investigated; alternative model editing methods can be explored.
Only a handful of text classification problems were investigated.
future_direction: Further investigation into the role and characteristics of complementary circuits.
Investigating the possibility of ideal circuits that can perform well for every specific task.
Exploring other techniques like ROME to edit complementary circuits without impacting primary circuits.
Creating more comprehensive datasets that capture a wider range of behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language model interpretability have identified circuits, critical subnetworks that replicate model behaviors, yet how knowledge is structured within these crucial subnetworks remains opaque. To gain an understanding toward the knowledge in the circuits, we conduct systematic knowledge editing experiments on the circuits of the GPT-2 language model. Our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in how circuits respond to editing attempts, the extent of knowledge distribution across network components, and the architectural composition of knowledge-bearing circuits. These findings offer insights into the complex relationship between model circuits and knowledge representation, deepening the understanding of how information is organized within language models. Our findings offer novel insights into the ``meanings'' of the circuits, and introduce directions for further interpretability and safety research of language models.

papers.title: There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction
papers.research_question: How different are the refusal directions when computed for different types of refusal behavior beyond safety, and how do these directions get expressed in the latent space such that they facilitate various styles of refusal under a similar intervention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal behavior in LLMs is mediated by multiple geometrically distinct activation-space directions, but linear steering along any refusal-related direction acts as a one-dimensional control knob for refusal, with differences primarily in refusal style. Sparse autoencoders reveal a structured internal representation with a shared core of refusal latents and a long tail of style-specific latents.
papers.conclusion: The internal structure of refusal is rich and structured, but linear control flattens this complexity, highlighting the limits of linear interpretability for aligned model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Different refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space.
Linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal–over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob.
The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses (style).
Sparse autoencoders uncover a structured internal representation: a small reusable core of shared refusal latents supplemented by a long tail of style- and domain-specific latents.
Linear interventions collapse over this structure, flattening mechanistic differences into uniform behavioral control.
papers.limitation:
The techniques could be misused to suppress refusal behavior and facilitate the generation of harmful content.
Linear steering collapses a rich internal refusal structure into a coarse behavioral knob, underscoring that such interventions are not suitable as principled safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Prior work argues that refusal in large language models is mediated by a single activation-space direction, enabling effective steering and ablation. We show that this account is incomplete. Across eleven categories of refusal and non-compliance, including safety, incomplete or unsupported requests, anthropomorphization, and over-refusal, we find that these refusal behaviors correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space. Yet despite this diversity, linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal to over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob. The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses.

papers.title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, bringing activation steering to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPBEND, a method that brings activation steering to fine-tuning by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, achieving state-of-the-art safety performance with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: REPBEND effectively enhances LLM safety by bending representations to separate safe and unsafe states, achieving state-of-the-art performance with minimal impact on general capabilities, offering a scalable safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
REPBEND achieves up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks.
REPBEND maintains general capabilities and usability, with minimal degradation on standard benchmarks.
REPBEND outperforms prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO in both black-box and white-box attacks.
REPBEND works best when applied to mid-to-later layers of the transformer.
REPBEND's loss function, which includes L2 norm, cosine similarity, and KL divergence terms, effectively separates safe and unsafe representations.
papers.limitation:
REPBEND requires a dataset of safe and unsafe prompts, which may not cover all possible harmful scenarios.
The method relies on the choice of layers and hyperparameters, which may need tuning for different models.
The transferability of LoRA for safety improvements remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring the transferability of LoRA adapters for safety across models.
Extending REPBEND to multimodal settings.
Investigating the theoretical foundations of representation bending.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools, but their inherent safety risks - ranging from harmful content generation to broader societal harms - pose significant challenges. These risks can be amplified by the recent adversarial attacks, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, and the increasing deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments. Existing safety-enhancing techniques, such as fine-tuning with human feedback or adversarial training, are still vulnerable as they address specific threats and often fail to generalize across unseen attacks, or require manual system-level defenses. This paper introduces RepBend, a novel approach that fundamentally disrupts the representations underlying harmful behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable solution to enhance (potentially inherent) safety. RepBend brings the idea of activation steering - simple vector arithmetic for steering model's behavior during inference - to loss-based fine-tuning. Through extensive evaluation, RepBend achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO, with up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks, all with negligible reduction in model usability and general capabilities.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Anchoring Refusal Direction: Mitigating Safety Risks in Tuning via Projection Constraint
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate safety risks posed by Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) while preserving task performance gains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a projection-constraint method (ProCon) that stabilizes the refusal direction in LLM hidden states during instruction fine-tuning, effectively mitigating associated safety risks without compromising task performance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that anchoring the refusal direction via a projection constraint method effectively mitigates safety risks introduced by instruction fine-tuning, providing an interpretability-driven approach for safer LLM tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal direction (r-direction), a key representation for safety, drifts during instruction fine-tuning, which is identified as a primary cause of emerging safety risks.
Applying a projection constraint on hidden states along the r-direction can mitigate this drift and reduce safety risks.
A warm-up strategy that applies strong constraints in early training stages and broadening the data distribution with safety-oriented samples further enhances the method's effectiveness and stability.
The proposed ProCon method, especially the enhanced ProCon_wu_safe variant, consistently outperforms strong baselines in mitigating safety risks across various LLMs and scenarios while preserving task performance.
papers.abstract: Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) has been widely adopted as an effective post-training strategy to enhance various abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, prior studies have shown that IFT can significantly compromise LLMs' safety, particularly their ability to refuse malicious instructions, raising significant concerns. Recent research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs has identified the refusal direction (r-direction) in the hidden states, which plays a pivotal role in governing refusal behavior. Building on this insight, our study reveals that the r-direction tends to drift during training, which we identify as one of the causes of the associated safety risks. To mitigate such drift, our proposed ProCon method introduces a projection-constrained loss term that regularizes the projection magnitude of each training sample's hidden state onto the r-direction. Our initial analysis shows that applying an appropriate constraint can effectively mitigate the refusal direction drift and associated safety risks, but remains limited by overall performance barriers. To overcome this barrier, informed by our observation of early-stage sharp drift and a data-driven perspective, we introduce a warm-up strategy that emphasizes early-stage strong constraints and broaden the data distribution to strengthen constraint signals, leading to an enhanced ProCon method. Experimental results under various datasets, scenarios, and LLMs demonstrate that our method can significantly mitigate safety risks posed by IFT while preserving task performance gains. Even compared with strong baselines, our method consistently delivers superior overall performance. Crucially, our analysis indicates that ProCon can contribute to stabilizing the r-direction during training, while such an interpretability-driven exploration of LLMs' internal mechanisms lays a solid foundation for future safety research.

papers.title: Towards Faithful Natural Language Explanations: A Study Using Activation Patching in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to measure the faithfulness of natural language explanations generated by large language models, using causal mediation techniques like activation patching.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Causal Faithfulness, a metric that uses activation patching to measure the faithfulness of natural language explanations by comparing causal attributions between explanations and answers, showing that aligned models produce more faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Causal Faithfulness is a promising step towards achieving true faithfulness in natural language explanations by leveraging activation patching to avoid out-of-distribution issues and provide deeper insights into model internals.
papers.key_findings:
Instruct-tuned models tend to produce more faithful explanations compared to pre-trained models.
Causal Faithfulness is a more theoretically sound framework for measuring faithfulness compared to existing surface-level methods like CC-SHAP and Counterfactual Faithfulness.
There is a positive correlation between the plausibility of explanations and their faithfulness as measured by CaF.
Activation patching reveals that models attribute higher causal importance to corrupted tokens and consider alternative answer choices during reasoning.
Patching across multiple layers does not significantly change faithfulness scores, but aggregating effects at token or layer levels shows variations.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational requirements due to the need for T · L forward passes for activation patching.
Token replacement requires edited tokens to be of equal length to the original tokens, which is complicated by varying tokenization schemes.
Activation patching primarily provides insights starting from the corrupted spans onward, limiting the scope of information revealed.
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic interpretability approaches to develop a more robust and reliable framework for assessing faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of generating persuasive Natural Language Explanations (NLEs) to justify their answers. However, the faithfulness of these explanations should not be readily trusted at face value. Recent studies have proposed various methods to measure the faithfulness of NLEs, typically by inserting perturbations at the explanation or feature level. We argue that these approaches are neither comprehensive nor correctly designed according to the established definition of faithfulness. Moreover, we highlight the risks of grounding faithfulness findings on out-of-distribution samples. In this work, we leverage a causal mediation technique called activation patching, to measure the faithfulness of an explanation towards supporting the explained answer. Our proposed metric, Causal Faithfulness quantifies the consistency of causal attributions between explanations and the corresponding model outputs as the indicator of faithfulness. We experimented across models varying from 2B to 27B parameters and found that models that underwent alignment tuning tend to produce more faithful and plausible explanations. We find that Causal Faithfulness is a promising improvement over existing faithfulness tests by taking into account the model's internal computations and avoiding out of distribution concerns that could otherwise undermine the validity of faithfulness assessments. We release the code in \url{https://github.com/wj210/Causal-Faithfulness}

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: CLUE: Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning Framework
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM unlearning by precisely localizing neurons responsible for forgetting and retaining, using circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CLUE, a framework that uses circuit discovery and CNF satisfiability to localize forget, retain, and conflict neurons for targeted unlearning, improving forget efficacy and retain utility.
papers.conclusion: CLUE offers more precise neuron localization and significantly outperforms existing methods in both forget efficacy and retain utility.
papers.key_findings:
CLUE outperforms existing localization methods in forget efficacy and retain utility with fewer modified parameters.
It successfully identifies forget, retain, and conflict neurons through CNF satisfiability of circuits.
The proportion of forget neurons increases and conflict neurons decreases after unlearning, indicating effective decoupling.
Circuit sparsity and faithfulness are correlated with unlearning efficacy.
CLUE provides more comprehensive interpretability by revealing neuron categories and their distributions.
papers.limitation:
The circuit is static and cannot dynamically reflect changes in key neurons during the fine-tuning process.
For multiple retain sets, the fine-tuning stage cannot provide targeted solutions for every possible conflict combination.
future_direction: Exploring the dynamics of circuits during parameter fine-tuning.
Developing editing methods other than fine-tuning for multiple retain sets.
papers.abstract: The LLM unlearning aims to eliminate the influence of undesirable data without affecting causally unrelated information. This process typically involves using a forget set to remove target information, alongside a retain set to maintain non-target capabilities. While recent localization-based methods demonstrate promise in identifying important neurons to be unlearned, they fail to disentangle neurons responsible for forgetting undesirable knowledge or retaining essential skills, often treating them as a single entangled group. As a result, these methods apply uniform interventions, risking catastrophic over-forgetting or incomplete erasure of the target knowledge. To address this, we turn to circuit discovery, a mechanistic interpretability technique, and propose the Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning framEwork (CLUE). This framework identifies the forget and retain circuit composed of important neurons, and then the circuits are transformed into conjunctive normal forms (CNF). The assignment of each neuron in the CNF satisfiability solution reveals whether it should be forgotten or retained. We then provide targeted fine-tuning strategies for different categories of neurons. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared to existing localization methods, CLUE achieves superior forget efficacy and retain utility through precise neural localization.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LoRA-Adapted Language Models for Nuclear Reactor Safety Applications
papers.research_question: How does LoRA adaptation alter neuron activation patterns in an LLM for a nuclear reactor safety domain, and what is the causal role of these altered neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a methodology for tracing domain expertise in a LoRA-adapted LLM to a sparse set of neurons and demonstrates that the model's expertise is an emergent property of a neural circuit, providing a pathway for nuclear-grade AI assurance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates a replicable methodology for moving beyond treating LLMs as opaque black boxes towards a mechanistic understanding of their function, offering a pathway to achieve nuclear-grade AI assurance by identifying, monitoring, and causally testing knowledge-bearing neural circuits.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning on a BWR dataset induced systematic changes in the activation patterns of a small set of neurons in the final MLP layer.
Silencing the entire group of six key neurons collectively caused a statistically significant degradation in BLEU score, while silencing most individual neurons did not, supporting a circuit-based view of knowledge encoding.
Qualitative analysis revealed distinct functional roles for key neurons, such as encoding core technical concepts (#1066, #1086), suppressing generalist language (#941), and representing procedural logic (#176).
The adapted model produced more concise and precise answers than the base model, as measured by a decrease in average answer length and an increase in BLEU score.
The findings suggest that verifying the integrity of distributed neural circuits, rather than individual components, is crucial for safety assurance in nuclear applications.
papers.limitation: The reliance on the BLEU score, while justified for measuring output precision, does not verify factual accuracy.
future_direction: Development of domain-specific evaluation metrics that can automatically verify technical correctness against a trusted knowledge base.
Extending the methodology to other critical nuclear systems, including Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) and advanced reactor designs.
Validating the approach across different model architectures, model scales, and technical documentation corpora.
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into safety-critical domains, such as nuclear engineering, necessitates a deep understanding of their internal reasoning processes. This paper presents a novel methodology for interpreting how an LLM encodes and utilizes domain-specific knowledge, using a Boiling Water Reactor system as a case study. We adapted a general-purpose LLM (Gemma-3-1b-it) to the nuclear domain using a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique known as Low-Rank Adaptation. By comparing the neuron activation patterns of the base model to those of the fine-tuned model, we identified a sparse set of neurons whose behavior was significantly altered during the adaptation process. To probe the causal role of these specialized neurons, we employed a neuron silencing technique. Our results demonstrate that while silencing most of these specialized neurons individually did not produce a statistically significant effect, deactivating the entire group collectively led to a statistically significant degradation in task performance. Qualitative analysis further revealed that silencing these neurons impaired the model's ability to generate detailed, contextually accurate technical information. This paper provides a concrete methodology for enhancing the transparency of an opaque black-box model, allowing domain expertise to be traced to verifiable neural circuits. This offers a pathway towards achieving nuclear-grade artificial intelligence (AI) assurance, addressing the verification and validation challenges mandated by nuclear regulatory frameworks (e.g., 10 CFR 50 Appendix B), which have limited AI deployment in safety-critical nuclear operations.

papers.title: SGM: Safety Glasses for Multimodal Large Language Models via Neuron-Level Detoxification
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether multimodal detoxification can be achieved directly at the neuron level without parameter updates or architectural changes, and if such interventions can remain efficient and transferable across models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SGM, a neuron-level multimodal detoxification framework that selectively suppresses toxic neurons in post-fusion layers without parameter updates, significantly reducing harmful outputs while preserving fluency and multimodal reasoning.
papers.conclusion: SGM substantially reduces toxic outputs on safety and toxicity benchmarks while maintaining response fluency, offering an efficient, interpretable, and low-overhead path toward safer and more robust MLLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SGM reduces the average harmful rate from 48.2% to 2.5% on safety benchmarks.
SGM preserves fluency and utility on general capability benchmarks like MM-VET with minimal degradation.
SGM is transferable across different MLLM architectures such as LLaVA and ShareGPT-4V.
SGM can be combined with existing detoxification methods like ECSO to form SGM⋆, achieving even stronger safety performance.
The method operates without any parameter updates, making it a low-cost, interpretable solution for toxicity control.
papers.limitation:
Transferability is currently limited to LLaVA and its variants; testing on architecturally different MLLMs is future work.
Detoxification focuses on MLP layers; extending it to attention or fusion modules remains future work.
Evaluation is primarily on MM-SafetyBench and MM-VET; incorporating more safety suites and attack types is needed.
Neuron-level suppression may cause false positives or over-refusals, affecting benign discussions of sensitive topics.
future_direction: Test SGM on architecturally different MLLMs (e.g., MiniGPT-4).
Extend detoxification to attention or fusion modules.
Incorporate more safety benchmarks and attack types for comprehensive evaluation.
papers.abstract: Disclaimer: Samples in this paper may be harmful and cause discomfort. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) enable multimodal generation but inherit toxic, biased, and NSFW signals from weakly curated pretraining corpora, causing safety risks, especially under adversarial triggers that late, opaque training-free detoxification methods struggle to handle. We propose SGM, a white-box neuron-level multimodal intervention that acts like safety glasses for toxic neurons: it selectively recalibrates a small set of toxic expert neurons via expertise-weighted soft suppression, neutralizing harmful cross-modal activations without any parameter updates. We establish MM-TOXIC-QA, a multimodal toxicity evaluation framework, and compare SGM with existing detoxification techniques. Experiments on open-source MLLMs show that SGM mitigates toxicity in standard and adversarial conditions, cutting harmful rates from 48.2\% to 2.5\% while preserving fluency and multimodal reasoning. SGM is extensible, and its combined defenses, denoted as SGM*, integrate with existing detoxification methods for stronger safety performance, providing an interpretable, low-cost solution for toxicity-controlled multimodal generation.

papers.title: Localizing Model Behavior with Path Patching
papers.research_question: How can we localize behaviors of neural networks to a subset of components or interactions, and how can we quantitatively test hypotheses about such localization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces path patching, a technique for expressing and quantitatively testing hypotheses that model behaviors are localized to specific sets of paths in a computational graph.
papers.conclusion: Path patching is an expressive formalism for localization claims that is both principled and sufficiently efficient to run on real models.
papers.key_findings:
The minimal explanation of induction heads is insufficient; a refined hypothesis including additional paths (e.g., from layer 0 heads to induction heads) explains more of the behavior.
Path patching can produce sparser and more precise localizations than causal tracing or zero ablation.
Head 1.5 in the studied model implements both induction and a distinct 'parroting' heuristic for repeating tokens.
Path patching attribution can identify specific inputs where a hypothesis is unfaithful, guiding iterative refinement.
papers.limitation:
Measures sufficiency rather than completeness; a set of paths with low AUE may not be the complete set of paths responsible for the behavior.
Provides no evidence about downstream tasks; low AUE does not guarantee the abstraction is useful for applications.
Makes no claims outside the tested distribution; low AUE on one dataset does not imply low AUE on a wider distribution.
Cannot reject all false hypotheses due to potential cancellation effects in metrics like difference in expected loss.
Cannot definitively prove hypotheses, as testing all possible inputs is infeasible.
Demonstrations are narrow in scope compared to the full range of behaviors exhibited by language models.
future_direction: Scaling path patching to state-of-the-art models.
Using interpretability to detect distribution shift.
Producing adversarial examples based on knowledge of model mechanisms.
Automating hypothesis search over combinations of paths.
papers.abstract: Localizing behaviors of neural networks to a subset of the network's components or a subset of interactions between components is a natural first step towards analyzing network mechanisms and possible failure modes. Existing work is often qualitative and ad-hoc, and there is no consensus on the appropriate way to evaluate localization claims. We introduce path patching, a technique for expressing and quantitatively testing a natural class of hypotheses expressing that behaviors are localized to a set of paths. We refine an explanation of induction heads, characterize a behavior of GPT-2, and open source a framework for efficiently running similar experiments.

papers.title: NeuroBreak: Unveil Internal Jailbreak Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak attacks exploit internal mechanisms in large language models to bypass safety alignments?
papers.core_contribution: NeuroBreak is a visual analytics system that unveils internal jailbreak mechanisms in LLMs by analyzing neuron-level safety mechanisms and enabling targeted fine-tuning to mitigate vulnerabilities.
papers.conclusion: NeuroBreak enhances expert understanding of LLM security mechanisms and supports precise alignment efforts through visual analysis and targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
NeuroBreak enables progressive exploration from macroscopic behavior to neuron-level mechanisms in jailbreak attacks.
It identifies safety neurons and categorizes them into functional archetypes based on toxicity vectors and activation patterns.
The system reveals that layers 15-28 encode discriminative harmful features with high probe accuracy.
Targeted fine-tuning of safety neurons using NeuroBreak improves model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
NeuroBreak provides visual evidence for neuron cooperation patterns and vulnerabilities in LLM safety mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on linear probing may miss nonlinear semantic shifts influencing adversarial behaviors.
Lack of dynamic adversarial interactions or real-time adaptation to evolving threats.
future_direction: Explore nonlinear probing techniques for more complex decision boundaries.
Incorporate dynamic adversarial training or online learning for real-time adaptation.
papers.abstract: In deployment and application, large language models (LLMs) typically undergo safety alignment to prevent illegal and unethical outputs. However, the continuous advancement of jailbreak attack techniques, designed to bypass safety mechanisms with adversarial prompts, has placed increasing pressure on the security defenses of LLMs. Strengthening resistance to jailbreak attacks requires an in-depth understanding of the security mechanisms and vulnerabilities of LLMs. However, the vast number of parameters and complex structure of LLMs make analyzing security weaknesses from an internal perspective a challenging task. This paper presents NeuroBreak, a top-down jailbreak analysis system designed to analyze neuron-level safety mechanisms and mitigate vulnerabilities. We carefully design system requirements through collaboration with three experts in the field of AI security. The system provides a comprehensive analysis of various jailbreak attack methods. By incorporating layer-wise representation probing analysis, NeuroBreak offers a novel perspective on the model's decision-making process throughout its generation steps. Furthermore, the system supports the analysis of critical neurons from both semantic and functional perspectives, facilitating a deeper exploration of security mechanisms. We conduct quantitative evaluations and case studies to verify the effectiveness of our system, offering mechanistic insights for developing next-generation defense strategies against evolving jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: SaLoRA: Safety-Alignment Preserved Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.research_question: What is the reason for safety alignment drop after LoRA fine-tuning, and how can we preserve safety alignment during low-rank adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SaLoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that preserves safety alignment by introducing a fixed safety module and task-specific initialization for low-rank adapters.
papers.conclusion: SaLoRA effectively preserves safety alignment during LoRA fine-tuning while maintaining performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning significantly alters the safety features of LLMs, leading to a drop in safety alignment.
SaLoRA, with its fixed safety module and task-specific initialization, preserves safety alignment while achieving comparable or better downstream task performance.
SaLoRA outperforms existing PEFT methods (LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA) and post-hoc alignment methods (Self-Reminder, InferAligner, Vaccine, Safe LoRA) in terms of harmful rate and utility.
Task-specific initialization for SaLoRA adapters improves convergence and performance compared to standard initialization.
SaLoRA maintains safety alignment even under jailbreak attacks (multi-GCG attack).
papers.abstract: As advancements in large language models (LLMs) continue and the demand for personalized models increases, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (e.g., LoRA) will become essential due to their efficiency in reducing computation costs. However, recent studies have raised alarming concerns that LoRA fine-tuning could potentially compromise the safety alignment in LLMs, posing significant risks for the model owner. In this paper, we first investigate the underlying mechanism by analyzing the changes in safety alignment related features before and after fine-tuning. Then, we propose a fixed safety module calculated by safety data and a task-specific initialization for trainable parameters in low-rank adaptations, termed Safety-alignment preserved Low-Rank Adaptation (SaLoRA). Unlike previous LoRA methods and their variants, SaLoRA enables targeted modifications to LLMs without disrupting their original alignments. Our experiments show that SaLoRA outperforms various adapters-based approaches across various evaluation metrics in different fine-tuning tasks.

papers.title: SORRY-Bench: Systematically Evaluating Large Language Model Safety Refusal
papers.research_question: How can we systematically evaluate large language models' safety refusal capabilities in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SORRY-Bench, a systematic benchmark for evaluating LLM safety refusal with a fine-grained taxonomy, balanced dataset, linguistic augmentations, and an efficient automated evaluator based on fine-tuned small LLMs.
papers.conclusion: SORRY-Bench provides a building block for systematic evaluations of LLMs’ safety refusal capabilities in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner.
papers.key_findings:
Prior safety evaluation datasets are imbalanced, over-representing certain fine-grained risk categories.
Linguistic mutations in prompts (e.g., different languages, writing styles) significantly affect model safety refusal performance.
Fine-tuned small LLMs (7B parameters) can achieve accuracy comparable to large LLMs like GPT-4 for safety evaluation, at lower computational cost.
Safety refusal varies widely across models; Claude-2 and Gemini-1.5 exhibit the most refusals, while Mistral models show high fulfillment rates.
Some risk categories (e.g., harassment, child-related crimes) are more frequently refused than others (e.g., legal advice, religion promotion).
papers.limitation:
The specialized safety evaluator model is not an ultimate gold standard and occasionally fails to align with human rubrics.
Due to resource and time constraints, the work did not conduct comprehensive testing across a spectrum of decoding parameters (e.g., varying temperatures).
papers.abstract: Evaluating aligned large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize and reject unsafe user requests is crucial for safe, policy-compliant deployments. Existing evaluation efforts, however, face three limitations that we address with SORRY-Bench, our proposed benchmark. First, existing methods often use coarse-grained taxonomies of unsafe topics, and are over-representing some fine-grained topics. For example, among the ten existing datasets that we evaluated, tests for refusals of self-harm instructions are over 3x less represented than tests for fraudulent activities. SORRY-Bench improves on this by using a fine-grained taxonomy of 44 potentially unsafe topics, and 440 class-balanced unsafe instructions, compiled through human-in-the-loop methods. Second, linguistic characteristics and formatting of prompts are often overlooked, like different languages, dialects, and more -- which are only implicitly considered in many evaluations. We supplement SORRY-Bench with 20 diverse linguistic augmentations to systematically examine these effects. Third, existing evaluations rely on large LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) for evaluation, which can be computationally expensive. We investigate design choices for creating a fast, accurate automated safety evaluator. By collecting 7K+ human annotations and conducting a meta-evaluation of diverse LLM-as-a-judge designs, we show that fine-tuned 7B LLMs can achieve accuracy comparable to GPT-4 scale LLMs, with lower computational cost. Putting these together, we evaluate over 50 proprietary and open-weight LLMs on SORRY-Bench, analyzing their distinctive safety refusal behaviors. We hope our effort provides a building block for systematic evaluations of LLMs' safety refusal capabilities, in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner. Benchmark demo, data, code, and models are available through https://sorry-bench.github.io.

papers.title: How to use and interpret activation patching
papers.core_contribution: Provides a summary of advice and best practices for using and interpreting activation patching, including the differences between denoising and noising, how to choose corrupted prompts, and the selection of appropriate metrics.
papers.conclusion: The paper summarizes recommendations for using activation patching: prefer it over ablations, carefully choose corrupted prompts to trace specific properties, understand the asymmetric roles of denoising and noising, and use continuous, linear metrics like logit difference for exploratory analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Denoising (clean→corrupt patching) tests whether patched activations are sufficient to restore model behavior, while noising (corrupt→clean patching) tests whether they are necessary to maintain behavior; these are not symmetric.
The choice of corrupted prompt is crucial, as it determines which properties of the model are traced; narrow variations are recommended for exploratory patching, while wide distributions are needed for confirmatory patching.
Logit difference is a preferred metric for activation patching because it is linear in the residual stream and avoids saturation and thresholding issues present in probability-based or discrete metrics.
Activation patching is more targeted and controlled than ablation techniques, as it replaces activations with cached values rather than zeroing them out, reducing out-of-distribution effects.
Path patching can be used to distinguish between direct connections and mediated effects in a circuit, helping to understand component interactions.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching is based on specific prompt distributions and does not make statements about model behavior outside these distributions.
Patching experiments do not guarantee minimality; a found circuit may not be the smallest set of components responsible for a behavior.
Negative components (e.g., attention heads that hurt performance when noised) and backup heads (OR-gate structures) can complicate circuit interpretation and recovery.
papers.abstract: Activation patching is a popular mechanistic interpretability technique, but has many subtleties regarding how it is applied and how one may interpret the results. We provide a summary of advice and best practices, based on our experience using this technique in practice. We include an overview of the different ways to apply activation patching and a discussion on how to interpret the results. We focus on what evidence patching experiments provide about circuits, and on the choice of metric and associated pitfalls.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: TraceRouter: Robust Safety for Large Foundation Models via Path-Level Intervention
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety in large foundation models by intervening at the path level to disconnect causal propagation circuits of harmful semantics, rather than suppressing isolated neurons?
