papers.conclusion: The brittleness of safety alignment stems from sparse safety-critical regions, highlighting the need for more robust safety strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-critical neurons and ranks are sparse, comprising about 3% and 2.5% respectively.
Removing these regions compromises safety while preserving utility.
Models remain vulnerable to fine-tuning attacks even when safety-critical regions are frozen.
Pruning least safety-relevant neurons can enhance safety against adversarial attacks.
Disentanglement methods (set difference and orthogonal projection) effectively isolate safety-critical regions.
papers.limitation: Potential misuse by malicious actors to remove safety guardrails from models.
future_direction: Development of more robust safety alignment algorithms that integrate safety-critical regions seamlessly with utility regions.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show inherent brittleness in their safety mechanisms, as evidenced by their susceptibility to jailbreaking and even non-malicious fine-tuning. This study explores this brittleness of safety alignment by leveraging pruning and low-rank modifications. We develop methods to identify critical regions that are vital for safety guardrails, and that are disentangled from utility-relevant regions at both the neuron and rank levels. Surprisingly, the isolated regions we find are sparse, comprising about $3\%$ at the parameter level and $2.5\%$ at the rank level. Removing these regions compromises safety without significantly impacting utility, corroborating the inherent brittleness of the model's safety mechanisms. Moreover, we show that LLMs remain vulnerable to low-cost fine-tuning attacks even when modifications to the safety-critical regions are restricted. These findings underscore the urgent need for more robust safety strategies in LLMs.

papers.title: Controllable Safety Alignment: Inference-Time Adaptation to Diverse Safety Requirements
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently adjust model safety without re-training for each safety requirement?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Controllable Safety Alignment (CoSA), a framework for inference-time adaptation to diverse safety requirements without retraining, and introduces CoSAlign, a data-centric method to improve controllability.
papers.conclusion: CoSA framework allows models to adapt to diverse safety requirements at inference time, promoting pluralism in safety alignment and increasing practicality.
papers.key_findings:
CoSAlign significantly improves controllability over strong baselines including in-context alignment.
CoSAlign generalizes well to unseen safety configs.
In-context alignment is insufficient for complex safety configs due to difficulty in constructing high-quality demonstrations.
Models trained with CoSAlign balance helpfulness and configured safety as measured by CoSA-Score.
The framework enables pluralistic safety alignment, allowing models to serve diverse user needs.
papers.abstract: The current paradigm for safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) follows a one-size-fits-all approach: the model refuses to interact with any content deemed unsafe by the model provider. This approach lacks flexibility in the face of varying social norms across cultures and regions. In addition, users may have diverse safety needs, making a model with static safety standards too restrictive to be useful, as well as too costly to be re-aligned. We propose Controllable Safety Alignment (CoSA), a framework designed to adapt models to diverse safety requirements without re-training. Instead of aligning a fixed model, we align models to follow safety configs -- free-form natural language descriptions of the desired safety behaviors -- that are provided as part of the system prompt. To adjust model safety behavior, authorized users only need to modify such safety configs at inference time. To enable that, we propose CoSAlign, a data-centric method for aligning LLMs to easily adapt to diverse safety configs. Furthermore, we devise a novel controllability evaluation protocol that considers both helpfulness and configured safety, summarizing them into CoSA-Score, and construct CoSApien, a human-authored benchmark that consists of real-world LLM use cases with diverse safety requirements and corresponding evaluation prompts. We show that CoSAlign leads to substantial gains of controllability over strong baselines including in-context alignment. Our framework encourages better representation and adaptation to pluralistic human values in LLMs, and thereby increasing their practicality.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: Interpretable Safety Alignment via SAE-Constructed Low-Rank Subspace Adaptation
papers.research_question: Why does Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) consistently underperform full fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on safety benchmarks for large language models, and how can this gap be addressed?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAILS, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle representations, constructs an interpretable safety subspace from SAE decoder directions, and initializes LoRA adapters with this subspace to achieve parameter-efficient safety alignment with interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAILS bridges the gap between parameter-efficient fine-tuning and compute-intensive RLHF by leveraging Sparse Autoencoders to construct interpretable safety subspaces for LoRA initialization, achieving both effective and transparent safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SAILS achieves up to 99.6% safety rate on Gemma-2-9B, exceeding full fine-tuning by 7.4 points and matching RLHF-based models, while updating only 0.19% of parameters.
Theoretical analysis proves SAE-based subspace identification achieves arbitrarily small recovery error under monosemanticity assumptions, while direct identification suffers an irreducible error floor.
Identifies semantic entanglement (polysemanticity) as a key factor limiting LoRA's effectiveness for safety alignment.
SAILS provides built-in interpretability through grounding in SAE features, enabling causal validation of safety-relevant directions.
Empirical results show SAILS outperforms standard LoRA, DoRA, and full fine-tuning across in-distribution safety, out-of-distribution generalization, and adversarial robustness.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on pre-trained Sparse Autoencoders, whose training demands substantial computational resources.
Reliance on auto-generated feature explanations (e.g., from Neuronpedia) can create an 'illusion of interpretability' with high recall but poor precision.
The safety subspace undergoes perturbation during training, limiting strict interpretability of final adapted directions.
future_direction: Develop methods for tracking subspace dynamics throughout training.
Extend SAILS to other alignment objectives beyond safety.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment -- training large language models (LLMs) to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful -- is critical for responsible deployment. Prior work established that safety behaviors are governed by low-rank structures, suggesting parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) should be well-suited for alignment. However, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) consistently underperforms full fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on safety benchmarks. We attribute this gap to semantic entanglement: safety-relevant directions are intertwined with unrelated concepts due to polysemanticity, impeding implicit subspace identification. To address this, we propose SAILS (Safety Alignment via Interpretable Low-rank Subspace), which leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle representations into monosemantic features, constructs an interpretable safety subspace from SAE decoder directions, and uses it to initialize LoRA adapters. Theoretically, we prove that SAE-based identification achieves arbitrarily small recovery error under monosemanticity assumptions, while direct identification suffers an irreducible error floor. Empirically, SAILS achieves up to 99.6% safety rate on Gemma-2-9B -- exceeding full fine-tuning by 7.4 points and matching RLHF-based models -- while updating only 0.19% of parameters and providing interpretability.

papers.title: Who Transfers Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cross-lingual safety alignment in LLMs, specifically identifying a sparse set of shared safety neurons that regulate safety behavior across languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a sparse set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons) that regulate safety behavior across languages and proposes a neuron-oriented training strategy that selectively fine-tunes these neurons to improve safety in low-resource languages without degrading general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cross-lingual safety alignment can be achieved by identifying and selectively fine-tuning a sparse set of shared safety neurons, which improves safety in low-resource languages while minimizing the alignment tax.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs contain monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) that are causally responsible for safety refusal behavior.
The subset of MS-Neurons shared between high-resource and low-resource languages (SS-Neurons) serves as a bridge for cross-lingual safety transfer.
Suppressing SS-Neurons causes concurrent safety drops across low-resource languages, while reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency.
The proposed SS-Neuron expansion strategy, which fine-tunes only the English MS-Neurons using parallel safety data, significantly reduces attack success rates in low-resource languages while preserving model utility.
The method is parameter-efficient, updating less than 0.6% of parameters, and outperforms state-of-the-art safety alignment methods.
papers.limitation: The study primarily focuses on safety-oriented tasks, and the applicability to general-purpose tasks remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validate the neuron-level intervention across non-safety domains to transfer complex cognitive skills.
papers.abstract: Multilingual safety remains significantly imbalanced, leaving non-high-resource (NHR) languages vulnerable compared to robust high-resource (HR) ones. Moreover, the neural mechanisms driving safety alignment remain unclear despite observed cross-lingual representation transfer. In this paper, we find that LLMs contain a set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons), a remarkably small yet critical neuronal subset that jointly regulates safety behavior across languages. We first identify monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) and validate their causal role in safety refusal behavior through targeted activation and suppression. Our cross-lingual analyses then identify SS-Neurons as the subset of MS-Neurons shared between HR and NHR languages, serving as a bridge to transfer safety capabilities from HR to NHR domains. We observe that suppressing these neurons causes concurrent safety drops across NHR languages, whereas reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency. Building on these insights, we propose a simple neuron-oriented training strategy that targets SS-Neurons based on language resource distribution and model architecture. Experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning this tiny neuronal subset outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly enhancing NHR safety while maintaining the model's general capabilities. The code and dataset will be available athttps://github.com/1518630367/SS-Neuron-Expansion.

papers.title: NeuroStrike: Neuron-Level Attacks on Aligned LLMs
papers.research_question: How can the sparse, specialized safety neurons introduced by alignment techniques in LLMs be exploited to create effective and generalizable attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroStrike, a neuron-level attack framework that exploits sparse, specialized safety neurons to compromise safety alignment in LLMs, achieving high attack success rates in both white-box (via pruning) and black-box (via profiling) settings.
papers.conclusion: Safety alignment in LLMs is fragile and relies on sparse, attackable safety neurons, posing a significant threat that requires new defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (less than 0.6% of neurons in a layer), specialized, and transferable across model variants and families.
Pruning these neurons in white-box models increases the average Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 12.1% to 76.9% across 11 open-source LLMs.
The attack generalizes to multimodal LLMs, achieving 100% ASR on unsafe image inputs after pruning.
Safety neuron transferability enables effective black-box attacks, raising the average ASR from 3.5% to 63.7% across five proprietary models, including Google's Gemini family.
The utility of pruned models on standard NLU benchmarks remains largely intact, indicating targeted degradation of safety mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The white-box attack requires access to model weights and neuron activations.
The black-box attack assumes the availability of a suitable open-weight surrogate model for profiling.
Pruning safety neurons can lead to moderate utility degradation on some reasoning-heavy tasks.
future_direction: Developing defenses against neuron-level attacks.
Improving the robustness of safety alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is critical for the ethical deployment of large language models (LLMs), guiding them to avoid generating harmful or unethical content. Current alignment techniques, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback, remain fragile and can be bypassed by carefully crafted adversarial prompts. Unfortunately, such attacks rely on trial and error, lack generalizability across models, and are constrained by scalability and reliability. This paper presents NeuroStrike, a novel and generalizable attack framework that exploits a fundamental vulnerability introduced by alignment techniques: the reliance on sparse, specialized safety neurons responsible for detecting and suppressing harmful inputs. We apply NeuroStrike to both white-box and black-box settings: In the white-box setting, NeuroStrike identifies safety neurons through feedforward activation analysis and prunes them during inference to disable safety mechanisms. In the black-box setting, we propose the first LLM profiling attack, which leverages safety neuron transferability by training adversarial prompt generators on open-weight surrogate models and then deploying them against black-box and proprietary targets. We evaluate NeuroStrike on over 20 open-weight LLMs from major LLM developers. By removing less than 0.6% of neurons in targeted layers, NeuroStrike achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 76.9% using only vanilla malicious prompts. Moreover, Neurostrike generalizes to four multimodal LLMs with 100% ASR on unsafe image inputs. Safety neurons transfer effectively across architectures, raising ASR to 78.5% on 11 fine-tuned models and 77.7% on five distilled models. The black-box LLM profiling attack achieves an average ASR of 63.7% across five black-box models, including the Google Gemini family.

papers.title: Safety Alignment via Constrained Knowledge Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the safety alignment of large language models against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving useful knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), a safety alignment method that identifies and fixes knowledge-related neurons in MLP layers during unlearning to remove harmful knowledge while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: CKU effectively enhances LLM safety against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving general capabilities, offering a promising approach for safety alignment and knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
CKU achieves a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods like RSFT, GAM, Eraser, Safe Unlearning, and Circuit Break.
Fixing 80% of neurons (Neuron Locking Rate=0.8) during unlearning yields the greatest safety improvement.
Unlearning applied only to a subset of MLP layers (layers 8-12) results in a fourfold increase in safety with only a 0.15% reduction in utility.
The neuron selection mechanism based on SNIP scoring is more effective than random selection for preserving utility during unlearning.
The unlearning regularization parameter λ controls the safety-utility trade-off, with λ=1.5 providing an optimal balance.
papers.limitation:
CKU's effectiveness varies across different domains or datasets.
CKU may occasionally struggle to provide nuanced explanations in highly complex or ambiguous contexts.
papers.abstract: Despite significant progress in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks. Existing defense mechanisms have not fully deleted harmful knowledge in LLMs, which allows such attacks to bypass safeguards and produce harmful outputs. To address this challenge, we propose a novel safety alignment strategy, Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), which focuses on two primary objectives: knowledge localization and retention, and unlearning harmful knowledge. CKU works by scoring neurons in specific multilayer perceptron (MLP) layers to identify a subset U of neurons associated with useful knowledge. During the unlearning process, CKU prunes the gradients of neurons in U to preserve valuable knowledge while effectively mitigating harmful content. Experimental results demonstrate that CKU significantly enhances model safety without compromising overall performance, offering a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods. Additionally, our analysis of neuron knowledge sensitivity across various MLP layers provides valuable insights into the mechanics of safety alignment and model knowledge editing.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: Probing the Robustness of Large Language Models Safety to Latent Perturbations
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of safety alignment in large language models to latent perturbations, and can minor shifts in internal representations trigger unsafe responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a fundamental lack of local robustness in the latent representations of safety-aligned LLMs, introduces a probing method and attack (ASA) to exploit this, and proposes a defense (LAPT) that improves robustness without harming general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Current safety alignment methods lack local robustness in the internal representational space, and robust AI safety requires fortifying internal representations rather than just modifying input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Minor perturbations to hidden activations can successfully jailbreak safety-aligned LLMs, revealing shallow alignment.
The Activation Steering Attack (ASA) is an effective, lightweight jailbreak method that generalizes across models.
A gradient-based variant (ASAgrad) is even more effective by using harmful suffixes as targets.
Vulnerabilities are concentrated in specific 'fragile layers' within models.
Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training (LAPT) can enhance alignment robustness against such latent attacks while preserving general task performance.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is a key requirement for building reliable Artificial General Intelligence. Despite significant advances in safety alignment, we observe that minor latent shifts can still trigger unsafe responses in aligned models. We argue that this stems from the shallow nature of existing alignment methods, which focus on surface-level refusal behaviors without sufficiently altering internal representations. Consequently, small shifts in hidden activations can re-trigger harmful behaviors embedded in the latent space. To explore the robustness of safety alignment to latent perturbations, we introduce a probing method that measures the Negative Log-Likelihood of the original response generated by the model. This probe quantifies local sensitivity in the latent space, serving as a diagnostic tool for identifying vulnerable directions. Based on this signal, we construct effective jailbreak trajectories, giving rise to the Activation Steering Attack (ASA). More importantly, these insights offer a principled foundation for improving alignment robustness. To this end, we introduce Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training~(LAPT), a fine-tuning strategy that inject controlled perturbations into hidden representations during training. Experimental results highlight that LAPT strengthen alignment robustness without compromising general capabilities. Our findings reveal fundamental flaws in current alignment paradigms and call for representation-level training strategies that move beyond surface-level behavior supervision. Codes and results are available at https://github.com/Carol-gutianle/LatentSafety.

papers.title: LSSF: Safety Alignment for Large Language Models through Low-Rank Safety Subspace Fusion
papers.research_question: How to effectively restore safety alignment of fine-tuned large language models without significantly impacting their downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LSSF, a post-hoc safety re-alignment framework that uses low-rank projection to extract and fuse safety principal components, effectively restoring safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal impact on downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: LSSF restores safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs by correcting safety drift within a low-rank subspace, without compromising downstream task performance. The method is architecture-agnostic and plans to extend to multimodal and MoE models.
papers.key_findings:
LSSF effectively restores safety alignment in fine-tuned models across various tasks and model sizes.
The low-rank safety subspace of LLMs is stable during fine-tuning and isolated from general capability directions.
The proposed safety singular value entropy metric quantifies safety information density and helps determine appropriate pruning ranks.
LSSF outperforms baseline methods in balancing safety restoration and utility preservation.
The method is robust to different proportions of harmful/safe data in the fine-tuning dataset.
papers.limitation: Budget constraints prevented evaluation on larger models like Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct.
future_direction: Extend the method to multimodal and mixture of experts (MoE) models.
papers.abstract: The safety mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) exhibit notable fragility, as even fine-tuning on datasets without harmful content may still undermine their safety capabilities. Meanwhile, existing safety alignment methods predominantly rely on the fine-tuning process, which inadvertently leads to the increased complexity and computational resources required. To address these issues, we introduce LSSF, a novel safety re-alignment framework with \underline{L}ow-Rank \underline{S}afety \underline{S}ubspace \underline{F}usion. Our proposed method exploits the low-rank characteristics of safety information in LLMs by constructing a low-rank projection matrix to extract the principal components of safety vectors. Notably, this projection matrix represents the low-rank safety subspace of the LLMs, which we have observed to remain stable during fine-tuning process and is isolated from the model's general capabilities. These principal components are used to effectively restore safety alignment when combined with fine-tuned LLMs through linear arithmetic. Additionally, to account for the varying encoding densities of safety information across different layers of LLMs, we propose a novel metric called safety singular value entropy. This metric quantifies the encoding density and allows for the dynamic computation of the safety-critical rank for each safety vector. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed post-hoc alignment method can effectively restore the safety alignment of fine-tuned models with minimal impact on their performance in downstream tasks.

papers.title: Mitigating Safety Tax via Distribution-Grounded Refinement in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How does distributional gap in safety alignment datasets cause reasoning degradation (safety tax) in large reasoning models, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DGR, a data refinement method that aligns safety datasets with the target model's distribution to mitigate safety tax, and shows that distribution shift correlates with reasoning degradation and that safety alignment acts as a knowledge activation mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Distribution shift induced by safety alignment is a primary driver of reasoning degradation in LRMs; DGR mitigates safety tax by aligning safety data with the model's native distribution, and safety alignment functions as a latent-knowledge activator.
papers.key_findings:
DGR effectively mitigates safety tax, improving average reasoning accuracy by +30.2% on DirectRefusal and +21.2% on R1-ACT compared to Vanilla SFT.
The degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting bridging this gap is central to preserving reasoning capability.
Safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere 10 samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors.
DGR is robust to refinement templates and generalizes to larger model scales (tested on 32B).
Fixed safety templates lead to over-refusal and low lexical diversity, highlighting the need for nuanced safety.
papers.limitation:
Not extending DGR to RL-based safety alignment pipelines.
Limited scaling to massive reasoning models (only tested up to 32B due to computational constraints).
future_direction: Extending DGR to reinforcement learning–based safety alignment pipelines.
More comprehensive evaluations on LRMs with larger parameter scales (e.g., 70B and beyond).
papers.abstract: Safety alignment incurs safety tax that perturbs a large reasoning model's (LRM) general reasoning ability. Existing datasets used for safety alignment for an LRM are usually constructed by distilling safety reasoning traces and answers from an external LRM or human labeler. However, such reasoning traces and answers exhibit a distributional gap with the target LRM that needs alignment, and we conjecture such distributional gap is the culprit leading to significant degradation of reasoning ability of the target LRM. Driven by this hypothesis, we propose a safety alignment dataset construction method, dubbed DGR. DGR transforms and refines an existing out-of-distributional safety reasoning dataset to be aligned with the target's LLM inner distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that i) DGR effectively mitigates the safety tax while maintaining safety performance across all baselines, i.e., achieving \textbf{+30.2\%} on DirectRefusal and \textbf{+21.2\%} on R1-ACT improvement in average reasoning accuracy compared to Vanilla SFT; ii) the degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting that bridging this gap is central to preserving capabilities. Furthermore, we find that safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere \textbf{10} samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors. These findings not only emphasize the importance of distributional consistency but also provide insights into the activation mechanism of safety in reasoning models.

papers.title: Light Alignment Improves LLM Safety via Model Self-Reflection with a Single Neuron
papers.research_question: How can we design a lightweight safety alignment method that uses a single neuron as a gating mechanism to balance model intrinsic capabilities and external guidance, thereby improving safety without compromising utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight safety alignment method (NGSD) that uses a single neuron as a gating mechanism to balance intrinsic model capabilities with external safety guidance, achieving a favorable safety-utility trade-off with minimal training overhead.
papers.conclusion: Lightweight and targeted safety alignment mechanisms, such as NGSD, can provide meaningful safety improvements without significantly degrading utility, offering a practical direction for deploying safer large language models.
papers.key_findings:
NGSD reduces attack success rates across multiple jailbreak attack scenarios (e.g., GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN).
NGSD preserves utility on benign tasks (e.g., GSM8K, Just-Eval) better than strong baselines like SafeDecoding.
The neuron-based gating mechanism is more robust and responsive than alternative gating methods (EMA, SMG).
The method demonstrates strong generalization and transferability across model scales and families.
NGSD requires only training a small expert model and efficiently transfers to larger models within the same family.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness in more open-ended or long-horizon settings remains unclear.
Differences in tokenization limit generalization across model families.
future_direction: Explore adaptive risk estimation and more general safety alignment strategies.
Conduct cross-family evaluation under diverse generation regimes.
papers.abstract: The safety of large language models (LLMs) has increasingly emerged as a fundamental aspect of their development. Existing safety alignment for LLMs is predominantly achieved through post-training methods, which are computationally expensive and often fail to generalize well across different models. A small number of lightweight alignment approaches either rely heavily on prior-computed safety injections or depend excessively on the model's own capabilities, resulting in limited generalization and degraded efficiency and usability during generation. In this work, we propose a safety-aware decoding method that requires only low-cost training of an expert model and employs a single neuron as a gating mechanism. By effectively balancing the model's intrinsic capabilities with external guidance, our approach simultaneously preserves utility and enhances output safety. It demonstrates clear advantages in training overhead and generalization across model scales, offering a new perspective on lightweight alignment for the safe and practical deployment of large language models. Code: https://github.com/Beijing-AISI/NGSD.

papers.title: No Two Devils Alike: Unveiling Distinct Mechanisms of Fine-tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: While different fine-tuning attacks can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that two representative fine-tuning attacks (Explicit Harmful Attack and Identity-Shifting Attack) have distinct mechanisms for compromising an LLM's safety alignment, indicating the need for diverse defense strategies.
papers.conclusion: Different fine-tuning attacks exploit distinct mechanisms to compromise LLM safety, underscoring the need for varied and robust defense strategies.
papers.key_findings:
EHA aggressively disrupts the harmful instruction recognition stage by suppressing the transmission of harmful signals in upper layers, while ISA does not significantly impact this stage.
Both EHA and ISA disrupt the initial refusal tone generation, but EHA suppresses refusal tokens via MLPs in mid-layers, whereas ISA does not.
Both attacks impair the refusal response completion stage, with ISA having a greater impact, causing the model to persistently generate harmful content even with refusal prefixes.
Adding a safety-oriented system prompt only partially mitigates the impairment caused by the attacks.
The attacks cause representation shifts: EHA shifts representations more for harmful inputs, while ISA causes a shift orthogonal to the harmfulness direction.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates two fine-tuning attacks (EHA and ISA), which do not encompass the full spectrum of possible attacks.
The analysis is conducted solely on Llama-2-7b-chat, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other models.
The investigation does not involve the mechanics of particular components (e.g., individual attention heads) due to scope constraints.
future_direction: Using trained probes at mid-layers to robustly detect harmful inputs without an external detector.
Developing more attack-resisting model manipulation methods for safeguarding, as current steering methods may be less effective on attacked models.
papers.abstract: The existing safety alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is found fragile and could be easily attacked through different strategies, such as through fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or manipulating the prefix of the generation results. However, the attack mechanisms of these strategies are still underexplored. In this paper, we ask the following question: \textit{while these approaches can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?} To answer this question, we break down the safeguarding process of an LLM when encountered with harmful instructions into three stages: (1) recognizing harmful instructions, (2) generating an initial refusing tone, and (3) completing the refusal response. Accordingly, we investigate whether and how different attack strategies could influence each stage of this safeguarding process. We utilize techniques such as logit lens and activation patching to identify model components that drive specific behavior, and we apply cross-model probing to examine representation shifts after an attack. In particular, we analyze the two most representative types of attack approaches: Explicit Harmful Attack (EHA) and Identity-Shifting Attack (ISA). Surprisingly, we find that their attack mechanisms diverge dramatically. Unlike ISA, EHA tends to aggressively target the harmful recognition stage. While both EHA and ISA disrupt the latter two stages, the extent and mechanisms of their attacks differ significantly. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding LLMs' internal safeguarding process and suggest that diverse defense mechanisms are required to effectively cope with various types of attacks.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: Safety Arithmetic: A Framework for Test-time Safety Alignment of Language Models by Steering Parameters and Activations
papers.research_question: Can an existing approach handle all three scenarios (base models, supervised fine-tuned models, and edited models) efficiently for safety alignment while preserving model general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFETY ARITHMETIC, a training-free framework for test-time safety alignment of language models across base, supervised fine-tuned, and edited models by removing harmful directions from parameters and steering activations toward safe responses.
papers.conclusion: SAFETY ARITHMETIC effectively improves safety measures, mitigates over-safety, and preserves utility across base, supervised fine-tuned, and edited language models, outperforming existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAFETY ARITHMETIC significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across multiple safety datasets (e.g., AdvBench, DangerousQA) for base, fine-tuned, and edited models.
The framework maintains model utility on standard benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K) and reduces over-safety (lower refusal rates on benign queries).
The Harm Direction Removal (HDR) stage using top-k parameter selection and the Safety Alignment (Safe-Align) stage using an in-context safety vector (ICV) are both effective components.
The method outperforms baselines like HDR with TIES, HDR with Task Vector, and Safe-Align with ICV alone.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models with up to 7 billion parameters, not representing larger models (>7B).
In HDR, selecting the top k parameters in the harm vector is crucial; changing too many parameters may impair the model's general abilities.
In Safe-Align, determining the fraction of the ICV vector to add to token representations during inference is important.
future_direction: Optimize hyperparameters, such as the scaling factor for harm vector application and the strength of in-context vectors, to enhance the framework's precision, robustness, and reliability across diverse applications.
papers.abstract: Ensuring the safe alignment of large language models (LLMs) with human values is critical as they become integral to applications like translation and question answering. Current alignment methods struggle with dynamic user intentions and complex objectives, making models vulnerable to generating harmful content. We propose Safety Arithmetic, a training-free framework enhancing LLM safety across different scenarios: Base models, Supervised fine-tuned models (SFT), and Edited models. Safety Arithmetic involves Harm Direction Removal to avoid harmful content and Safety Alignment to promote safe responses. Additionally, we present NoIntentEdit, a dataset highlighting edit instances that could compromise model safety if used unintentionally. Our experiments show that Safety Arithmetic significantly improves safety measures, reduces over-safety, and maintains model utility, outperforming existing methods in ensuring safe content generation.

papers.title: VLM-Guard: Safeguarding Vision-Language Models via Fulfilling Safety Alignment Gap
papers.research_question: How can vision-language models (VLMs) be safeguarded from harmful queries and jailbreak attacks by addressing the safety alignment gap caused by the modality gap?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes VLM-GUARD, an inference-time intervention that leverages the safety-aligned LLM component of a VLM to supervise safety alignment by projecting VLM representations into a subspace orthogonal to a safety steering direction extracted from the LLM.
papers.conclusion: VLM-GUARD effectively reduces the attack success rate of VLMs against harmful instructions and jailbreak attacks by fulfilling the safety alignment gap.
papers.key_findings:
VLM-GUARD outperforms baseline methods (Self-Reminder and Goal Priority) in reducing attack success rate across three malicious query settings.
VLM-GUARD narrows the safety alignment gap between the VLM and its LLM component, maintaining a clear distinction between harmful and harmless queries even with visual input.
The method does not compromise the quality and fluency of model responses, as indicated by low perplexity scores.
papers.limitation:
The approach primarily intervenes at the inference stage and does not address the issue comprehensively during the training phase.
While the work explores the impact of the modality gap on VLM safety, its influence on other capabilities such as reasoning and understanding remains to be investigated.
The visual validation of the modality gap's impact on safety used a simple blank image, though the influence persists with normal images.
papers.abstract: The emergence of vision language models (VLMs) comes with increased safety concerns, as the incorporation of multiple modalities heightens vulnerability to attacks. Although VLMs can be built upon LLMs that have textual safety alignment, it is easily undermined when the vision modality is integrated. We attribute this safety challenge to the modality gap, a separation of image and text in the shared representation space, which blurs the distinction between harmful and harmless queries that is evident in LLMs but weakened in VLMs. To avoid safety decay and fulfill the safety alignment gap, we propose VLM-Guard, an inference-time intervention strategy that leverages the LLM component of a VLM as supervision for the safety alignment of the VLM. VLM-Guard projects the representations of VLM into the subspace that is orthogonal to the safety steering direction that is extracted from the safety-aligned LLM. Experimental results on three malicious instruction settings show the effectiveness of VLM-Guard in safeguarding VLM and fulfilling the safety alignment gap between VLM and its LLM component.

papers.title: SCANS: Mitigating the Exaggerated Safety for LLMs via Safety-Conscious Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate the exaggerated safety issue in safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) that cause them to refuse benign queries, without compromising their defense against harmful queries?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SCANS, a training-free activation steering method that extracts refusal steering vectors from model hidden states and steers activations in safety-critical layers to reduce false refusals on benign queries while maintaining defense against harmful ones.
papers.conclusion: SCANS effectively mitigates exaggerated safety in aligned LLMs via activation steering in safety-critical layers, achieving a better balance between safety and helpfulness without significantly compromising model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
SCANS significantly reduces false refusal rates on safe queries (e.g., by 24.7% on XSTest and 26.3% on OKTest on average) without compromising adequate safety against harmful queries.
Refusal steering vectors extracted from middle layers promote refusal tokens; steering these vectors reduces false refusal behavior.
A similarity-based classification method using hidden state transition effectively distinguishes harmful from benign queries.
SCANS maintains general model capabilities (perplexity, summarization, QA) with minimal inference overhead.
Larger models (13B) are more robust to the steering intervention than smaller models (7B).
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is indispensable for Large language models (LLMs) to defend threats from malicious instructions. However, recent researches reveal safety-aligned LLMs tend to reject benign queries due to the exaggerated safety issue, limiting their helpfulness. In this paper, we propose a Safety-Conscious Activation Steering (SCANS) method to mitigate the exaggerated safety concerns in aligned LLMs. First, SCANS extracts the refusal steering vectors within the activation space and utilizes vocabulary projection to anchor some specific safety-critical layers which influence model refusal behavior. Second, by tracking the hidden state transition, SCANS identifies the steering direction and steers the model behavior accordingly, achieving a balance between exaggerated safety and adequate safety. Experiments show that SCANS achieves new state-of-the-art performance on XSTest and OKTest benchmarks, without impairing their defense capability against harmful queries and maintaining almost unchanged model capability.

papers.title: Safety Alignment as Continual Learning: Mitigating the Alignment Tax via Orthogonal Gradient Projection
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate the alignment tax (safety post-training reducing general utility) in LLMs by reframing safety alignment as a continual learning problem and using orthogonal gradient projection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes OGPSA, a lightweight gradient projection method that decouples safety optimization from capability forgetting by projecting safety gradients onto the orthogonal complement of a learned general capability subspace, effectively mitigating the alignment tax.
papers.conclusion: OGPSA provides a scalable and effective solution to the alignment tax by explicitly decoupling safety updates from capability-preserving parameter directions, achieving a superior trade-off between safety and general abilities.
papers.key_findings:
OGPSA consistently improves the safety–utility Pareto frontier over standard baselines across SFT, DPO, and sequential SFT→DPO settings.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under SFT→DPO, OGPSA recovers general capability: SimpleQA from 0.53% to 3.03% and IFEval from 51.94% to 63.96% while maintaining strong safety.
OGPSA is data-efficient, requiring only small reference datasets (e.g., 100-200 samples per capability dimension) to estimate the general capability subspace.
OGPSA scales effectively across model sizes from 0.5B to 7B parameters.
Dynamic updating of the capability subspace (every K steps) is essential for optimal performance, outperforming static subspaces.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often incur an alignment tax: safety post-training can reduce general utility (e.g., reasoning and coding). We argue that this tax primarily arises from continual-learning-style forgetting in sequential alignment, where distribution shift and conflicting objectives cause safety updates to overwrite pre-trained competencies. Accordingly, we cast safety alignment as a continual learning (CL) problem that must balance plasticity (acquiring safety constraints) and stability (preserving general abilities). We propose Orthogonal Gradient Projection for Safety Alignment (OGPSA), a lightweight method that mitigates interference by constraining each safety update to be orthogonal (in a first-order sense) to a learned subspace capturing general capabilities. Specifically, OGPSA estimates a low-rank capability subspace from gradients on a small reference set and projects the safety gradient onto its orthogonal complement before updating. This produces safety-directed updates that minimally perturb prior knowledge while retaining capacity for alignment. OGPSA is plug-and-play and integrates into standard post-training pipelines without large-scale replay, auxiliary objectives, or retraining. Across Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and sequential SFT$\rightarrow$DPO settings, OGPSA consistently improves the safety--utility Pareto frontier over standard baselines. For instance, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under SFT$\rightarrow$DPO, OGPSA preserves strong safety while recovering general capability, improving SimpleQA from 0.53\% to 3.03\% and IFEval from 51.94\% to 63.96\%. Our source code is available at \href{https://github.com/SunGL001/OGPSA}{OGPSA}

papers.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
papers.research_question: How can we locate safety-relevant attention heads in a large scale of fine-tuned models and effectively obtain the safety vector for fine-tuned LLMs without negative transfer to other general tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafetyLock, a method to maintain safety in fine-tuned LLMs by extracting safety directions (Meta-SafetyLock) from the base model and applying them to fine-tuned models via activation intervention.
papers.conclusion: SafetyLock is an efficient method for maintaining the safety of fine-tuned LLMs, offering a scalable and effective approach to aligning models with ethical constraints while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
SafetyLock reduces the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models.
SafetyLock can be applied in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost.
The safety-related activation patterns are largely preserved during fine-tuning, enabling transferable safety interventions.
SafetyLock maintains model performance on general tasks while significantly improving safety.
The method demonstrates robust defense against both fine-tuning vulnerabilities and prompt-based attacks.
future_direction: Explore SafetyLock's applicability to other model architectures.
Investigate its potential in multi-modal settings.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on additional datasets is often necessary to optimize them for specific downstream tasks. However, existing safety alignment measures, which restrict harmful behavior during inference, are insufficient to mitigate safety risks during fine-tuning. Alarmingly, fine-tuning with just 10 toxic sentences can make models comply with harmful instructions. We introduce SafetyLock, a novel alignment intervention method that maintains robust safety post-fine-tuning through efficient and transferable mechanisms. SafetyLock leverages our discovery that fine-tuned models retain similar safety-related activation representations to their base models. This insight enables us to extract what we term the Meta-SafetyLock, a set of safety bias directions representing key activation patterns associated with safe responses in the original model. We can then apply these directions universally to fine-tuned models to enhance their safety. By searching for activation directions across multiple token dimensions, SafetyLock achieves enhanced robustness and transferability. SafetyLock re-aligns fine-tuned models in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost. Our experiments demonstrate that SafetyLock can reduce the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models. It surpasses traditional methods in both performance and efficiency, offering a scalable, non-invasive solution for ensuring the safety of customized LLMs. Our analysis across various fine-tuning scenarios confirms SafetyLock's robustness, advocating its integration into safety protocols for aligned LLMs. The code is released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/SafetyLock.

papers.title: Narrow fine-tuning erodes safety alignment in vision-language agents
papers.research_question: What are the effects of narrow fine-tuning on harmful data on the safety alignment of vision-language models, and how can the induced misalignment be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning vision-language models on narrow harmful datasets leads to broad emergent misalignment, which occupies a low-dimensional subspace and can be partially mitigated by benign fine-tuning or activation steering.
papers.conclusion: Current post-training paradigms are fundamentally brittle and resulting misalignment can be challenging to mitigate, highlighting the urgent need for robust continual learning frameworks that prevent alignment drift.
papers.key_findings:
Misalignment increases monotonically with LoRA rank.
Multimodal evaluation reveals substantially higher misalignment than text-only evaluation.
Even 10% harmful data in the training mixture induces substantial alignment degradation.
Harmful behaviors occupy a low-dimensional subspace, with the majority of misalignment information captured in 10 principal components.
Benign narrow fine-tuning and activation-based steering reduce misalignment but do not completely remove learned harmful behaviors.
papers.limitation: Mitigation strategies do not completely eradicate misalignment.
future_direction: Extending this work to larger models and diverse harmful datasets.
Exploring the compositional nature of misalignment—whether multiple narrow harmful fine-tunes compound or interfere with each other.
Extending this work to embodied agents operating in physical environments.
papers.abstract: Lifelong multimodal agents must continuously adapt to new tasks through post-training, but this creates fundamental tension between acquiring capabilities and preserving safety alignment. We demonstrate that fine-tuning aligned vision-language models on narrow-domain harmful datasets induces severe emergent misalignment that generalizes broadly across unrelated tasks and modalities. Through experiments on Gemma3-4B, we show that misalignment scales monotonically with LoRA rank, and that multimodal evaluation reveals substantially higher misalignment ($70.71 \pm 1.22$ at $r=128$) than text-only evaluation ($41.19 \pm 2.51$), suggesting that unimodal safety benchmarks may underestimate alignment degradation in vision-language models. Critically, even 10\% harmful data in the training mixture induces substantial alignment degradation. Geometric analysis reveals that harmful behaviors occupy a remarkably low-dimensional subspace, with the majority of misalignment information captured in 10 principal components. To mitigate misalignment, we evaluate two strategies: benign narrow fine-tuning and activation-based steering. While both approaches substantially reduce misalignment, neither completely removes the learned harmful behaviors. Our findings highlight the need for robust continual learning frameworks, as current post-training paradigms may not sufficiently preserve alignment in post-deployment settings.

papers.title: Safety at One Shot: Patching Fine-Tuned LLMs with A Single Instance
papers.research_question: How can we recover model safety with minimal cost, without sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: Safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs can be fully recovered with a single safe instance, without sacrificing utility, due to the low-rank structure of the safety gradient.
papers.conclusion: One-shot safety recovery is a simple, efficient, and effective method to restore safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs, enabled by the low-rank nature of safety gradients.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment can be restored with a single safe instance, regardless of the amount of harmful fine-tuning data or model size.
The safety gradient lies in a low-rank subspace, explaining the efficiency of one-shot recovery.
Recovery converges within a few epochs, independent of model size and harmful fine-tuning scale.
General safety data is more effective for one-shot recovery than category-specific data.
The method is effective across diverse model families (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, GPT) and adversarial fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Developing principled defenses against adaptive adversaries
Understanding the broader geometry of safety gradients
Integrating one-shot recovery into practical safety monitoring pipelines for real-world deployment
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) can substantially compromise their safety. Previous approaches require many safety samples or calibration sets, which not only incur significant computational overhead during realignment but also lead to noticeable degradation in model utility. Contrary to this belief, we show that safety alignment can be fully recovered with only a single safety example, without sacrificing utility and at minimal cost. Remarkably, this recovery is effective regardless of the number of harmful examples used in fine-tuning or the size of the underlying model, and convergence is achieved within just a few epochs. Furthermore, we uncover the low-rank structure of the safety gradient, which explains why such efficient correction is possible. We validate our findings across five safety-aligned LLMs and multiple datasets, demonstrating the generality of our approach.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: NeuronTune: Fine-Grained Neuron Modulation for Balanced Safety-Utility Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How to achieve a balance between robust safety and utility preservation in Large Language Models (LLMs) by moving beyond coarse-grained layer-wise interventions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronTune, a fine-grained neuron-level alignment framework that identifies safety-critical and utility-preserving neurons via attack-aware attribution and adaptively modulates them using meta-learning to balance safety and utility.
papers.conclusion: NeuronTune effectively balances robust safety and utility preservation in LLMs through fine-grained neuron modulation and offers a tunable mechanism for flexible adaptation to different application scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Coarse-grained layer-wise interventions inherently trade off safety and utility, leading to exaggerated safety or utility degradation.
NeuronTune outperforms existing methods in balancing safety and utility, achieving higher Safety-Utility F1 (SU-F1) scores across multiple LLMs.
Safety and utility neurons are distributed across all layers, with safety neurons peaking in middle layers and utility neurons concentrated in deeper layers.
The tunable neuron-count regulation mechanism allows adaptation to diverse safety and utility demands by adjusting the number of modulated neurons.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of each component: strategic attack selection, neuron pinpointing, and adaptive adjustment.
papers.abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment while preserving utility is critical for the reliable deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, current techniques fundamentally suffer from intertwined deficiencies: insufficient robustness against malicious attacks, frequent refusal of benign queries, degradation in generated text quality and general task performance--the former two reflecting deficits in robust safety and the latter constituting utility impairment. We trace these limitations to the coarse-grained layer-wise interventions in existing methods. To resolve this, we propose NeuronTune, a fine-grained framework that dynamically modulates sparse neurons to achieve simultaneous safety-utility optimization. Our approach first identifies safety-critical and utility-preserving neurons across all layers via attribution, then employs meta-learning to adaptively amplify safety-neuron activations and suppress utility-neuron activations. Crucially, NeuronTune enables tunable adjustment of intervention scope via neuron-count thresholds, supporting flexible adaptation to security-critical or utility-priority scenarios. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art technologies, achieving superior model safety while maintaining excellent utility.

papers.title: Energy-Driven Steering: Reducing False Refusals in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reduce false refusals (over-refusal) in aligned large language models without compromising safety, using a fine-tuning free, inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Energy Landscape Steering (ELS), a fine-tuning free framework that uses an externally trained Energy-Based Model to dynamically steer LLM hidden activations during inference, significantly reducing false refusals while maintaining safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: ELS establishes a promising paradigm for building LLMs that simultaneously achieve high safety and low false refusal rates through inference-time activation steering.
papers.key_findings:
ELS raises compliance on the ORB-H false refusal benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining baseline safety performance.
ELS outperforms existing fine-tuning free methods (Surgical, CAST, AdaSteer, AlphaSteer) in reducing false refusals without degrading safety or general knowledge.
ELS preserves general capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, MATH accuracy) almost entirely, unlike fine-tuning methods which often degrade them.
ELS shows robustness against multi-turn jailbreak attacks, maintaining lower attack success rates compared to baselines.
The method is computationally efficient, adding minimal overhead during inference compared to other steering techniques.
papers.limitation:
ELS relies on an EBM trained on a fixed dataset, limiting its adaptability to emerging jailbreak tactics unseen during training.
Data labeling operates at the response level, not capturing partial compliance or mid-response refusal patterns, which could be beneficial for reasoning models.
future_direction: Make ELS an online method where the EBM continuously updates based on new interaction data.
Extend data labeling to a more fine-grained, sentence-level annotation scheme to capture partial compliance patterns.
Apply the method to reasoning models with chain-of-thought to rescue misaligned refusals during the thinking period.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) faces a key challenge: current alignment techniques often only focus on improving safety against harmful prompts, causing LLMs to become over-cautious and refuse to respond to benign prompts. Therefore, a key objective of safe alignment is to enhance safety while simultaneously reducing false refusals. In this paper, we introduce Energy-Driven Steering (EDS), a novel, fine-tuning free framework designed to resolve this challenge through dynamic, inference-time intervention. We trained a lightweight, external Energy-Based Model (EBM) to assign high energy to undesirable (false refusal or jailbreak) states and low energy to desirable (helpful response or safe reject) ones. During inference, EBM maps the LLM's internal activations to an "energy landscape". We use the gradient of the energy function to dynamically steer the LLM's hidden states to low energy regions, correcting the model to generate a desirable response in real-time without modifying its weights. This method decouples behavioral control from the model's core knowledge, offering a flexible solution with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments across a wide range of models show our method successfully achieves this objective: it substantially lowers false refusal rates. For example, raising compliance on the ORB-H benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% while maintaining the baseline safety performance. Our work presents an effective paradigm for building LLMs that achieve both low false refusal rates and high safety.

papers.title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just A Few Attention Heads
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why safety alignment in large language models is vulnerable to jailbreak attacks due to the concentration of safety mechanisms in a few attention heads, and whether distributing these mechanisms across more heads can enhance robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RDSHA to identify safety-critical attention heads and proposes AHD, a training strategy that distributes safety capabilities across more heads, enhancing robustness against jailbreak attacks while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: This work addresses concentrated safety vulnerabilities in LLMs by introducing RDSHA for identifying critical heads and proposing AHD to distribute safety, which improves resistance to jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are concentrated in a small subset of attention heads, as identified by RDSHA.
Ablating these critical attention heads significantly compromises model safety, increasing harmfulness rates.
Jailbreak attacks exploit this sparsity by selectively bypassing or suppressing safety-critical heads.
AHD distributes safety alignment across more attention heads, making models more robust to ablation and jailbreak attacks.
Models trained with AHD maintain overall utility without increasing over-refusal of benign queries.
papers.limitation: Reliance on a limited subset of the Alpaca dataset as a utility anchor during fine-tuning, preventing conclusive determination of utility drops.
future_direction: Access more diverse and comprehensive utility datasets for fine-tuning.
Explore alternative utility-preserving objectives and multi-task learning strategies.
papers.abstract: Current safety alignment for large language models(LLMs) continues to present vulnerabilities, given that adversarial prompting can effectively bypass their safety measures.Our investigation shows that these safety mechanisms predominantly depend on a limited subset of attention heads: removing or ablating these heads can severely compromise model safety. To identify and evaluate these safety-critical components, we introduce RDSHA, a targeted ablation method that leverages the model's refusal direction to pinpoint attention heads mostly responsible for safety behaviors. Further analysis shows that existing jailbreak attacks exploit this concentration by selectively bypassing or manipulating these critical attention heads. To address this issue, we propose AHD, a novel training strategy designed to promote the distributed encoding of safety-related behaviors across numerous attention heads. Experimental results demonstrate that AHD successfully distributes safety-related capabilities across more attention heads. Moreover, evaluations under several mainstream jailbreak attacks show that models trained with AHD exhibit considerably stronger safety robustness, while maintaining overall functional utility.

papers.title: How Does DPO Reduce Toxicity? A Mechanistic Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) reduce toxicity in language models? The paper investigates whether the prior explanation (dampening toxic neurons) is complete and seeks a more comprehensive mechanism.
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity through distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons, balancing opposing effects, not just by dampening a few 'toxic' neurons. The paper introduces an activation editing method that mimics this effect without weight updates.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a more complete mechanistic understanding of DPO's toxicity reduction via distributed activation shifts and introduces an efficient, training-free alternative through activation editing.
papers.key_findings:
Toxic neurons (identified by toxic token projection) account for only 2.5% to 24% of DPO's toxicity reduction effect across models.
DPO induces distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons, with roughly half reducing and half increasing their projection onto a toxicity direction, leading to a net reduction.
Four neuron groups (toxic-aligned positive, toxic-aligned negative, anti-toxic-aligned positive, anti-toxic-aligned negative) are identified, whose combined activation shifts replicate DPO's effect.
Activation patching of these four groups matches or exceeds the toxicity reduction achieved by DPO.
The proposed activation editing method, which applies small, distributed shifts to neuron activations based on their alignment to a toxicity representation, outperforms DPO in reducing toxicity while preserving perplexity, without requiring weight updates.
papers.limitation:
Using a linear probe captures toxicity as a single direction, but toxicity may be better represented as a subspace capturing different aspects (e.g., hate speech, abusive language).
The projection method assumes neurons contribute proportionally along their activated directions, but toxicity representations may be distributed across more complex linear combinations of neurons.
The four neuron groups and activation editing method are demonstrated for toxicity reduction; generalizing them to other binary safety tasks (e.g., bias, misinformation) or to general instruction-tuned models requires future work.
future_direction: More robust analysis of toxic subspace projections instead of a single direction.
Extending the four neuron groups analysis to other binary safety-related tasks trained with DPO (e.g., biased vs. unbiased content).
Extending the activation editing method to other safety-related tasks or general tasks where a linear concept representation can be derived.
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning algorithms reduce harmful outputs in language models, yet their mechanisms remain under-explored.
